title: Cold and wet today
title_target: Tá sé fuar agus fliuch inniu
goal: Making negatives and questions with the verb *tá*, answering without words for "yes" and "no", using adjectives, and talking about the weather.
bekal: answer questions without a word for "yes" or "no"
put adjectives after the noun and strengthen them with *an-*

dialogs.title: Comhrá — Bricfeasta sa chistin
dialogs.intro: Budi's first morning at Máire's house. It's raining outside, and breakfast is waiting on the kitchen table.

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Dia duit ar maidin, a Bhudi. An bhfuil tú tuirseach?
lines.id: Good morning, Budi. Are you tired?
lines.literal: God to-you on morning, O Budi. Q is you tired?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Níl. Tá mé go breá. Tá an teach seo an-chiúin.
lines.id: No. I'm great. This house is very quiet.
lines.literal: is-not. is I in-a-fine-way. is the house this very-quiet.

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Tá sé ciúin, cinnte. An bhfuil ocras ort?
lines.id: It's quiet, all right. Are you hungry?
lines.literal: is it quiet, certain. Q is hunger on-you?

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Tá arán úr agus im ar an mbord. Tá an tae te fós.
lines.id: There's fresh bread and butter on the table. The tea's still hot.
lines.literal: is bread fresh and butter on the table. is the tea hot still.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Go hálainn. Cén sórt aimsire atá ann inniu?
lines.id: Lovely. What's the weather like today?
lines.literal: beautiful-ly. what sort of-weather that-is in-it today?

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Tá sé fuar agus fliuch. Tá sé ag cur báistí.
lines.id: It's cold and wet. It's raining.
lines.literal: is it cold and wet. is it at putting of-rain.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: An bhfuil sé fuar i gcónaí i nGaillimh?
lines.id: Is it always cold in Galway?
lines.literal: Q is it cold in always in Galway?

lines.speaker: Máire:
lines.text: Níl sé fuar i gcónaí, ach tá sé fliuch go minic!
lines.id: It's not always cold, but it's often wet!
lines.literal: is-not it cold in always, but is it wet often-ly!

lines.speaker: Seán:
lines.text: Tá an aimsir go dona inniu, ach tá an bricfeasta go hiontach.
lines.id: The weather's bad today, but the breakfast is wonderful.
lines.literal: is the weather bad-ly today, but is the breakfast wonderful-ly.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tá an t-arán an-bhlasta. Go raibh maith agat.
lines.id: The bread is really tasty. Thank you.
lines.literal: is the bread very-tasty. may-there-be good at-you.

notes: **Níl isn't "not" plus "tá".** It's one whole word that replaces all of *tá*, fused from *ní* (not) and *fuil* (another form of *tá*). So *Tá mé tuirseach* becomes *Níl mé tuirseach*, not "ní tá mé". A third form appears in questions: *An bhfuil mé tuirseach?* All three are the same verb.

**Tá and Níl are your "yes" and "no".** Irish has no words for either. Asked *An bhfuil ocras ort?*, you answer by repeating the verb: *Tá* or *Níl*. Asked with a different verb, you answer with that verb — *An ólann tú tae?* gets *Ólaim* or *Ní ólaim*. The habit carried over into Irish English: "I do, yeah." "It is."

**An-chiúin, an-bhlasta — an intensifier that brings séimhiú.** The prefix *an-* means "very", is written with a hyphen, and always lenites the next letter: *ciúin* → *an-chiúin*, *blasta* → *an-bhlasta*, *mór* → *an-mhór*. Its sibling *ró-* means "too" and works the same way: *róthe* (too hot), *rófhuar* (too cold).

**Tá ocras orm — hunger sits on a person.** Irish doesn't say "I'm hungry" but "there's hunger on me". The pattern covers almost every physical feeling and emotion: *tart* (thirst), *tuirse* (tiredness), *áthas* (joy), *brón* (sadness), *fearg* (anger). The preposition is *ar*, which swallows the pronoun to make *orm, ort, air, uirthi*. Unit 8 covers it in full.

sections.title: Tá, Níl, An bhfuil — three faces of one verb

blocks.text: All you need are three forms, and none of them changes for different people. Only the pronoun changes.

How to say them: *tá* = TAW, *níl* = NEEL, *an bhfuil* = an WIL. Look at *bhfuil* — this is the urú (eclipsis) you saw in the pronunciation chapter: *bh* is written in front of *f*, and the *f* stops being pronounced. Drop the first two letters and you get *fuil*, which the dictionary lists under the verb *bí*.

blocks.title: Don't look for a word for "yes" — there isn't one
items: Asked *An bhfuil tú go maith?*, answer *Tá* (not "sea", not "yeah").

For questions about **identity** that use the verb *is*, the answer is different again: *Sea* and *Ní hea*. That's Unit 6. For now, every question starting with *An bhfuil …* is answered *Tá* or *Níl*.
To be emphatic, repeat the whole sentence: *Tá, tá mé go maith.* This sounds the most natural and is never wrong.

blocks.text: The opposite of English (but just like French or Spanish): the adjective comes **after** its noun. *Teach mór* — "house big", a big house. *Tae te* — "tea hot", hot tea. Flip the order in your head once and it soon feels natural.

An adjective standing after *tá* doesn't change at all: *Tá an teach mór*, *Tá na tithe mór*. Adjectives only change form when they're attached directly to a feminine noun or a plural noun — that's covered in Unit 4.

blocks.title: Two typical mistakes
items: **Don't write *an* without the hyphen.** *An mhaith* means "the good" with the article; *an-mhaith* means "very good". The hyphen changes the meaning.

**An adjective after *go* isn't strengthened — it becomes an adverb.** *Tá sé maith* means "it's good (a thing)"; *Tá sé go maith* means "it's in a good way". When asking how people are, always use *go maith*.
*Go* adds an **h** when the next word begins with a vowel: *go hiontach*, *go hálainn*, *go holc* (badly).

sections.title: An aimsir — the weather, the conversation that never fails

blocks.text: In Ireland the weather isn't empty small talk; it really does change four times a day, and people really do talk about it. These thirteen sentences will see you through the whole year.

The word *ann* in the last sentences literally means "in it" and says that something **exists, is out there**. *Tá gaoth ann* = "there's wind in it", i.e. "it's windy". The same form is used for seasons: *Tá an samhradh ann* — "it's summer now".

blocks.title: Four seasons, and why one name is already familiar
items: *Samhain* — the name for November and the start of winter in the old calendar — is the root of **Halloween**, which in Ireland is still called *Oíche Shamhna*, "Samhain night".
*Deireadh Fómhair* literally means "end of autumn" and is the name for October; *Meán Fómhair*, "middle of autumn", is September.

exercises.prompt: Turn these into questions, then answer as shown in brackets.
Fill in the right adjective (te, fuar, blasta, mór, ciúin, fliuch).

answers: Níl mé tuirseach. — Níl sé fuar inniu. — Níl an tae te. — Níl siad sásta. — Níl ocras orm. — Níl an aimsir go breá.
An bhfuil tú go maith? Tá. — An bhfuil sé fliuch? Níl. — An bhfuil an bricfeasta réidh? Tá. — An bhfuil Máire anseo? Níl. — An bhfuil tart ort? Tá. — An bhfuil siad tuirseach? Níl.
